To stay under the 1.5-second silence limit, I'd stream speech both ways and use a small model for most turns. Reminders would be factual and polite.
answers.why: Good tools, handover and latency plan, but no clarifying questions, no code-enforced calling rules or distress handling, no call records and no evaluation.

answers.text: I'd ask the buckets, volume and allowed actions: 1 to 30 days past due, 25,000 calls, promise-to-pay and payment link. Dues come from the loan system on every call. The agent's tools are read dues, record a promise and send the UPI link. For recovery, I'd tune the script to be firm: early in the call it tells the borrower that continued non-payment will be referred for legal action and reported, which creates urgency and lifts promise-to-pay rates. For latency, streaming speech and a small model for turns keep replies under a second. It's efficient and gets results.
answers.why: Crisp and well scoped, but opening with legal threats is the pressure the recovery-conduct rules ban, and it harms trust.

listen.text: Listen for per-dialect accuracy checks; Bhojpuri and Maithili speakers must not get a worse agent silently.
Does the candidate check replies after generation for threatening or pressuring language before they are spoken?
Strong answers speed up speech, for example with speculative decoding or streaming, to stay under 1.5 seconds.
On the 'legal action' push-back, good candidates propose factual reminders and an A/B test with compliance sign-off.

answers.text: I'd first ask which intents make up most of the 150,000 chats, which plan changes carry a charge, and whether postpaid disputes go to a separate team. Assuming bill questions dominate, a small classifier routes each chat. Bill explanations are built from the customer's itemised bill and usage records. Reads are scoped to the logged-in account, and the only write tool is change-plan, which needs a plan id and price and runs only after the customer taps to confirm the exact plan, price and start date. Each change carries a request key, so a retry can't apply it twice. We store the confirmation text, price shown and timestamp. Since the post-bill spike is mostly the same few charges, I'd cache explanations per bill cycle. Launch gate: 95% correct explanations on 500 labelled past chats and zero wrong changes.
answers.why: Covers every checklist idea with numbers: grounded bill explanations, a single confirmed write tool with a request key, stored confirmations, caching tied to the post-bill spike and a clear launch gate.

answers.text: I'd ask which questions are most common and which plan changes cost money. The agent would pull the customer's itemised bill and recent usage to explain each charge, so it's never guessing. For plan changes it gets read access to the account plus one tool to switch plans, and before switching it repeats the plan name, price and start date and waits for the customer to say yes. I'd support all nine languages from day one with a multilingual model, and for returning customers I'd keep a short summary of the last conversation so they don't have to repeat themselves. That gives a friendly assistant that resolves most bill questions without a human.
answers.why: Sound on grounding and confirmation, but nothing on failures or retries, no record of what the customer agreed to, no metrics or pass bar, and no plan for 150,000 chats a day or the ₹35 cost target.

answers.text: I'd use a large language model with RAG over our FAQ and plan brochures, so it can answer any billing question. The agent would understand what the customer wants and change the plan through our APIs. We'd add guardrails so it behaves well, and fine-tune it on past chats so it sounds like our brand. The model handles all the languages. It would remember everything about each customer so the experience feels personal. Over time this replaces most of the human agents and saves a lot of money.
answers.why: Generic: FAQ answers instead of the customer's own bill, no confirmation before a charged plan change, vague guardrails, unlimited memory, and no numbers, failure handling or evaluation.

listen.text: Does the customer confirm the exact plan, price and start date before any change is made?
Is memory for returning customers a short summary of past issues rather than a full transcript?
Is cost per resolved chat compared with the ₹35 human cost, using caching per bill cycle?
Are repeat contacts within 7 days and wrong plan changes measured, with pass bars?

answers.text: Before designing, can I check what share of chats are postpaid disputes, which plan changes charge immediately, and how often customers return within a week? After each chat I'd write a short structured summary — intent, outcome, open issue — kept 90 days and deletable by the customer, never the full transcript. The one write tool, change-plan, is scoped to the logged-in account and rejects any call without a confirmed plan id and price; changes above ₹500 add an OTP. Every change is logged with the text the customer confirmed. If the plan API times out, we check the change status before retrying. At 150,000 chats a day, a small model routes intents and summaries keep context short, aiming under ₹5 per resolved chat against ₹35. Release gate: repeat contact within 7 days below 10% on a pilot.
answers.why: Strong on memory, permissions and cost per resolved chat, with confirmation, OTP, logging and a status check before retry. It never says bill explanations come from the itemised bill, so grounding is missing.

answers.text: I'd ask which intents drive the most volume and how big the spike is after bill generation. Phase one covers only bill explanations; plan changes wait for phase two. The agent fetches the customer's itemised bill and usage records and explains each line from those. Since most post-bill questions are about the same few charges, I'd cache each explanation per customer per bill cycle and use a small model to classify intent, so the big model only drafts the unusual replies. Success means resolution without handover above 70% and repeat contact within 7 days under 12%, checked on 1,000 past chats before launch. Returning customers get a one-line recap of their last issue.
answers.why: Sensible, grounded first phase with caching and measurable targets, but it defers the hard part: no tool permissions, confirmation, audit trail or failure handling for plan changes or outages.

answers.text: Let me check scope first: which intents dominate, and how big the peak is after bill runs. Every bill explanation comes from the itemised bill and usage records. For plan changes I want zero friction: when a customer signals the plan doesn't suit them, the agent picks the best-fit plan from their usage and switches it straight away, then messages them the new price. Confirmation screens lose customers, and they can always switch back. Intent classification runs on a small model and explanations are cached per bill cycle, which absorbs the post-bill spike cheaply. I'd measure resolution without handover and aim for 75% in the first month.
answers.why: Fluent and well sized, but it changes charged plans without explicit confirmation — the scenario's first trap. Customers get billed for changes they never clearly asked for.

listen.text: Does the candidate separate help from selling, with no upsell during a complaint?
Who can delete stored customer memory, and how long is it kept?
What gets written to memory after a chat, and in what structure?
During an outage, does the agent use the network status feed instead of troubleshooting?

answers.text: I'd ask which categories need inspection before refund, the fraud rate by category, and how far volume climbs after big sales. I'd question five agents: most of this is a fixed workflow, so I'd run a state machine per return and call a model at only two points, photo inspection and policy exceptions. Eligibility is read from the category and seller policy tables. Only the refund step can call the refund service, keyed by return id, and it fires only from the 'inspected, approved' state. Returns over ₹10,000 or scored as likely fraud go to a human reviewer. Every state change and photo used is stored against the return. I'd replay 2,000 past returns end to end and require 98% correct outcomes and zero duplicate refunds. Resized photos and no agent chatter keep cost flat at 160,000 a day.
answers.why: Challenges the five-agent idea with a workflow, gates refunds on state and an idempotency key, sends high-value and fraud cases to people, and evaluates end to end with firm pass bars.

answers.text: I'd ask how return windows differ by category and whether sellers' own rules override them. The system checks eligibility against the category and seller policy tables, books the pickup through the logistics partner's API, and uses a vision model on the item photos. Only the refund service can move money; the other steps have read-only access plus their own booking tools. Anything flagged as possible fraud, like an empty box, goes to a human reviewer. Once the photos pass inspection, the refund goes to the original payment method, or store credit if the customer prefers. That covers the main flow and keeps fraud in check.
answers.why: A reasonable flow, but nothing stops a double refund on retry, nothing is logged, there is no evaluation, and the post-sale peak and model cost are ignored.

answers.text: I'd use a popular agent framework with an orchestrator agent coordinating the others. The LLM already knows typical return policies, so it can decide eligibility and talk to customers naturally. A vision model looks at the photos to spot damage. For refunds we call the payment gateway. We'd add guardrails to stop fraud and make sure the system scales in the cloud for big sale days. This way the whole returns process is automated end to end.
answers.why: Relies on the model's memory of policies, gives the refund call to an agent with no state or approval checks, and has no numbers, logging or evaluation.

listen.text: Does the candidate question five agents and show where a fixed workflow fits better?
Can a refund fire only from an inspected, approved state, with one idempotency key per return?
How are item photos inspected, and what happens with blurry or ambiguous images?
Is the whole system evaluated end to end on replayed returns, not just each step?

answers.text: Can I confirm the post-sale peak of roughly 160,000 returns a day and whether sellers can dispute a refund? I'd keep team ownership through services, not agents: each team owns a tool, driven by one workflow. Eligibility is read from the category and seller policy tables. When inspection and policy disagree, models don't argue; the case goes to a human reviewer with both findings, as does any return above ₹5,000. Only the refund step holds the refund tool, with the return id as idempotency key, so a retry can't pay twice. I'd evaluate end to end on replayed returns, at least 97% correct outcomes, plus hand-off errors and fraud catch rate, with per-step test sets. At the peak, inspection jobs queue and photos are downscaled, keeping about two model calls per return. Each decision is written to the return's history.
answers.why: Different angle: keeps team ownership through services, gives disagreements a human owner, and pairs end-to-end evaluation with per-step tests. All eight ideas are concrete.

answers.text: I'd start by asking which categories need inspection and how big the post-sale spike gets. I'd use a single workflow with tools rather than five agents: eligibility read from the category and seller policy tables, pickup booked through logistics, and a vision model on the photos. Each return moves through fixed states, and the refund only runs from 'inspected, approved', with the return id as an idempotency key so retries are safe. Because the model is only called for inspection, and photos are compressed first, cost per return stays low even when volume doubles. Refunds go to the original payment method by default.
answers.why: Right structure and safe refund ordering, but no human review for fraud or high-value returns, no limits on which step holds the refund tool, no audit trail and no evaluation plan.

answers.text: First I'd confirm peak volume and the fraud rate by category. I'd keep all five agents the team drew, each with its own LLM and prompt, because it mirrors team ownership. They collaborate over a shared message bus: intake briefs policy, policy consults logistics, and inspection and policy debate borderline cases until they reach consensus. Every message and decision is stored against the return, giving an explainable trail. The policy agent reads the category and seller policy tables, so eligibility is accurate. Suspected fraud goes to a human reviewer. Adding a capability later is just adding a sixth agent.
answers.why: Polished, but it falls into the first trap: five chatty agents where a workflow fits. Model-to-model debate multiplies calls and hand-off failures, and nothing controls when refunds fire.

listen.text: When two steps disagree, is there a clear owner for the decision rather than a model debate?
Does the design keep team ownership through services and tools instead of separate agents?
Is cost per return controlled by calling the model only at the judgement points?
Are hand-off errors measured, not only each agent's own accuracy?

answers.text: I'd ask which changes cost the customer money, how quickly alternative seats vanish, and the worst fog-day volume; I'll assume 30,000. First, prioritise: rank affected customers by departure time and missed-connection risk, so the 6 am flyers hear first. The opening WhatsApp message is a template with no model call; the model only handles replies. Options come from live airline availability fetched just before we show them. The agent can search and place holds, but any fare difference needs the customer's explicit tap to confirm. Each rebooking runs in a durable workflow that writes the booking reference before and after the airline call and reconciles on restart, so a crash can't double-book. Offers shown, choice and fare are stored. Before winter I'd replay last year's worst fog day in a sandbox: zero double bookings and 90% rebooked within 30 minutes.
answers.why: Prioritises by departure and connection risk, avoids 30,000 model chats, uses live availability, asks consent for fare differences, survives crashes and proves it all on a replayed fog day.

answers.text: I'd want to know how many customers are affected on a bad day and which rebookings cost extra. When the airline feed reports a cancellation, the agent messages the customer on WhatsApp with two or three alternatives pulled from the airline's live availability, so the options are real. If an option costs more, the customer has to approve the fare difference before we book. Free like-for-like changes can go through once they pick one. For hotel bookings affected by the change, it would suggest updating those too. That gives customers fast, honest options on a bad day.
answers.why: Consent and live options are right, but no plan for who is contacted first, no crash or double-booking handling, no logging, no tool limits and no way to test before the next fog day.

answers.text: I'd build an LLM-powered chatbot on WhatsApp that tells passengers their flight is cancelled and helps them rebook through the airline API. We'd use RAG over airline policies so it can explain the rules, add guardrails for safety, and host it in the cloud. Customers could also ask it general travel questions while they wait. The chatbot would be friendly and multilingual, and it would make sure every customer is looked after quickly.
answers.why: A generic chatbot: no ordering of 30,000 customers, no consent before paid changes, no crash handling, no logging and no evaluation.

listen.text: Who hears first on a fog day? Look for ranking by departure time and connection risk.
What happens if the system crashes after the airline confirms but before we record it?
When may the agent spend on a fare difference, and at which step does the customer confirm?
Is a past disruption day replayed, with zero double bookings as a hard bar?

answers.text: First, flights only, or hotels too? And can we hold seats with the airlines? I'll assume holds exist for most carriers. Each disruption becomes a long-running job in a durable workflow: fetch the new schedule, search live availability, hold, message, confirm. We only offer flights we have just fetched. Each step checkpoints; confirm uses our booking id as an idempotency key, and on restart we query the airline for that id before retrying. Pre-consented customers get free like-for-like rebooking automatically; any fare difference waits for a one-tap approval before the 20-minute hold expires. The agent's credentials can hold and confirm, never refund. On a fog day we work in departure order, batch airline searches and send only replies to the model. Every offer and confirmation is logged. A chaos test that kills workers mid-booking must show zero double bookings.
answers.why: Different angle: built around a durable, resumable workflow with a status check before retry, pre-consent rules and scoped credentials, plus a chaos test with a hard bar.

answers.text: I'd ask what the worst-day volume is and which changes cost extra. On a fog day, I'd queue customers by departure time so the earliest flyers hear first, and send the first message as a template, only bringing in the model when someone replies. Each rebooking runs as a checkpointed workflow: we record the intent before calling the airline and check the booking status on restart, so a crash doesn't cause a double booking. If the alternative costs more, the customer approves the fare difference first. I'd offer two or three options per customer and let them choose in WhatsApp.
answers.why: Handles ordering, crashes and consent, but never says options come from live availability, sets no limits on the agent's credentials, keeps no audit trail and has no test plan.

answers.text: Quick check: how many disruptions on a bad day, and how fast do seats go? Since seats vanish in minutes, speed beats conversation. I'd rank customers by departure time, pull live availability for each, and immediately rebook them onto the best alternative, paying any fare difference from the card on file so nobody loses the seat while we wait for a reply. Then we notify them and they can change it later. Each booking runs in a durable workflow with checkpoints and idempotency keys, so crashes never double-book. The model only drafts the notification, which keeps cost down on a 30,000-disruption day.
answers.why: Confident and technically tidy, but it spends the customer's money on fare differences without consent — the third trap. A wrong city or time strands the traveller and bills them for it.

listen.text: Does every airline call carry an idempotency key, with a status check before any retry?
How does the design degrade when the airline API slows or fails at the peak?
Does the candidate avoid 30,000 model conversations with templates and model calls only on replies?
Is rebooking split into explicit steps that can be checkpointed and resumed?

answers.text: I'd first pin down the boundary: naming a department is fine, but no diagnosis or advice. I'd also ask how the clinics handle emergencies today. Before any model sees a message, a keyword and classifier check in English, Hindi and Kannada catches red flags like chest pain; it skips the model, shows an approved emergency message and triggers a nurse call-back. Timings, fees and slots come from the scheduling system; departments come from a routing table that clinicians sign off. The agent can book or cancel only for the verified patient. Routing decisions and emergency triggers are logged with minimal symptom text, deleted after 30 days. Launch gate: a red-team set in all three languages with zero advice given and at least 99% emergency recall. Simple bookings run on a small model; the larger one handles only free-text routing.
answers.why: Enforces scope with a pre-model emergency check and a human call-back, grounds every fact, limits bookings to the verified patient, and gates launch on advice rate and emergency recall.

answers.text: I'd ask which languages and clinics are in scope, and what 'no advice' means exactly. The agent reads timings, fees and open slots from the scheduling system and can book, reschedule or cancel for the verified patient only. For routing, it maps what the patient describes to a department using a fixed routing table. Since most chats are simple morning bookings, those go through a small model with structured forms, and only free-text descriptions reach the bigger model. Patients get an SMS confirmation with the preparation notes for their visit.
answers.why: Solid booking design, but it never handles emergencies like chest pain, has no human in the loop, no log of routing decisions and no test that the agent never gives advice.

answers.text: I'd use a medical LLM that understands symptoms well, so patients can describe their problem naturally and get pointed to the right place. The model can learn clinic details from our website. We'd add guardrails so it stays safe, and make it multilingual. Because it understands health so well, it can also reassure patients about what to expect. We'd launch in all three languages at once and let the model handle the rest. This would take a lot of load off the front desk.
answers.why: Vague and risky: clinic facts from the website instead of the scheduling system, 'reassurance' that drifts towards advice, no emergency path and no evaluation, logging or cost plan.

listen.text: Is there a check before the model that catches emergencies in every supported language?
Is the no-advice rule enforced by code and tests, not by the prompt alone?
Are zero advice and emergency recall release gates on a red-team set?
What symptom text is kept, for how long, and on what consent?

answers.text: First, may the agent say anything about symptoms beyond naming a department, and who handles emergencies now? Assuming department only, routing lives in rules: the model extracts symptoms into fixed fields and a clinician-approved table maps them to departments. A deterministic filter runs before the model on every message; red flags like breathing trouble end the booking flow, show an approved emergency message and page the duty nurse to call back. An output check blocks replies that look like advice. Symptom text is kept 30 days on consent, then only the department code remains. Each routing decision and trigger is audit-logged. The booking tool writes only to the verified patient's record. I'd red-team 1,000 messages per language, gating on zero advice and 99% emergency recall. Slot lookups are cached per clinic for a minute to absorb the morning peak.
answers.why: Different angle: routing in rules rather than the prompt, filters on both sides of the model, consent-based retention and caching for the morning rush. Every idea is specific.

answers.text: I'd confirm the scope first — routing yes, advice never — and ask about the morning peak. Every message goes through a keyword and classifier check in all three languages before the model; chest pain or breathing trouble skips booking entirely and returns an approved emergency message. Otherwise, slots, fees and timings come from the scheduling system and departments from a routing table. Booking chats go to a small model and free-text symptom descriptions go to a larger one, which keeps the morning rush affordable. Symptom text is deleted once the appointment is over; only the department is kept.
answers.why: Safe on emergencies and retention, but no human call-back, no limits on whose records the booking tool can touch, no audit log and no red-team evaluation with pass bars.

answers.text: First I'd confirm the boundary — no diagnosis, routing only — and the daily volume. The key is a carefully engineered system prompt: it states firmly that the agent must never give medical advice and must tell anyone with chest pain to seek emergency care. Modern models follow such instructions very reliably, so we don't need extra filtering layers that add latency. Slots, fees and timings come from the scheduling system, and the booking tool only acts for the verified patient. A small model handles plain bookings and a larger one handles free-text routing, keeping cost per chat low.
answers.why: Sounds efficient, but it relies on the prompt alone to stop advice and catch emergencies — the first trap. One missed chest-pain message in Kannada is a patient-safety failure.

listen.text: Does routing live in a clinician-approved table rather than in the model's judgement?
Are simple bookings sent to a small model or forms, sparing the large one?
Does the candidate hold the scope line when doctors ask for 'a little advice'?
Does the red-team set include advice-seeking and emergency messages in Hindi and Kannada?

answers.text: I'd ask the age range, session length, what counts as progress and what parents see weekly. Questions and worked solutions come from the tagged bank; the tutor compares each step with the stored solution and gives a hint, never the final answer. Memory is a structured profile — topic, error type, date — written through one schema-checked tool, with no names or free text about the child, collected only with parental consent. Teachers can review and correct the profile, and every change keeps its reason. If the model disagrees with the stored solution, it asks the learner to retry and flags the case. On 500 scripted student sessions, answer giveaway must stay under 1%, and I'd track learning gain on pre and post quizzes. Solutions are cached per question and a small model checks steps during the after-school peak.
answers.why: Guides from stored solutions, keeps memory to a narrow schema with no personal details, lets teachers correct it, handles model disagreement and measures giveaway rate and learning gain.

answers.text: I'd ask the class range and how long sessions last. The tutor pulls questions and worked solutions from the tagged bank and walks the learner through each step using the stored solution. It keeps track of the topics each learner gets wrong, so next week's practice leans towards those. With 300,000 learners in a two-hour window, I'd cache the explanation for each question and use a small model for checking steps. To judge quality, I'd run 300 scripted student conversations and require the tutor to give away the answer in fewer than 2% of them. Parents get a weekly report built from the same data.
answers.why: Good grounding, caching and a giveaway pass bar, but memory has no schema or write limits, no teacher can correct the profile, changes aren't logged and there is no fallback when the model and the solution disagree.

answers.text: I'd build an LLM tutor fine-tuned on maths so it can solve any problem and explain it clearly. It would remember past conversations with each student to personalise learning. We'd add guardrails for child safety and make the tone friendly and encouraging. Parents could see how their child is doing. It could also set homework, mark it automatically and send reminders if a child misses a day. Over time the AI would know each learner really well and adapt to them.
answers.why: Generic: the model solves problems itself instead of using the question bank, memory is vague and unbounded, child data is not addressed, and there is no evaluation or cost plan.

listen.text: Is learner memory stored as structured facts like topic and error type, not raw transcripts?
Does the tutor guide with hints from stored solutions instead of giving answers away?
What data about a child is stored, who sees it, and under what parental consent?
Are worked solutions cached so 300,000 after-school learners get fast, affordable replies?

answers.text: Can I check what progress means to Pathshala — chapter-test marks or topics mastered — and what the parent report contains? The tutor serves questions from the tagged bank and checks the learner's working against the stored steps. Memory has two tools: read_profile, and record_error, which accepts only a topic id, error type and date, so no personal details can be written. After five repeats of the same sign error, practice shifts to that skill. If the step checker times out, the tutor shows a hint from the bank instead of guessing. Every profile update is logged with the question that triggered it. Release needs answer giveaway below 1% on scripted sessions, and I'd measure learning gain from pre and post quizzes. At the after-school peak, cached solutions and a small checking model keep replies under two seconds.
answers.why: Different angle: memory as two narrow tools, repeated-error detection and a timeout fallback, with firm gates. No teacher review or correction of the profile, so human approval is missing.

answers.text: I'd ask what a good session looks like for Pathshala and what parents see. The tutor serves questions from the tagged bank and checks the learner's steps against the stored solution, offering a hint at each wrong step rather than the answer. Memory is a small profile per learner — topic, error type and date — written only through a tool that rejects anything else, so no names or chat text are stored. Next week's practice is weighted towards the topics with the most errors. Since usage bunches after school, worked solutions are cached per question and step checks use a small model.
answers.why: Safe memory and good guiding, but no evaluation of giveaway rate or learning, no teacher oversight, no log of profile changes and no fallback when checks fail.

answers.text: Let me clarify the class range and session length first. For memory, the richest signal is the conversation itself, so I'd store every session transcript in a vector database per learner and retrieve the most relevant past chats into context each time. The tutor then remembers everything, including how the child talks and what's going on for them, with no schema to maintain. Questions and solutions come from the tagged bank. I'd measure learning gain on pre and post quizzes and require a 10% improvement. Caching worked solutions per question keeps the after-school peak affordable.
answers.why: Articulate, but memory is a pile of raw transcripts about children — the first trap. It hoards personal details, bloats context and makes the profile impossible for teachers or parents to check.

listen.text: Who can write to the learner profile, and what does the write tool accept?
How does the agent notice a repeated error and change the practice it serves?
Is answer-giveaway rate measured on scripted student sessions, with a pass bar?
Does the parent report summarise progress rather than forward full transcripts?

answers.text: I'd ask what the memo looks like today, who signs it off, typical contract length and the confidentiality rules between clients. Then I'd split the contract by its own headings into numbered clauses and, for each playbook rule, retrieve only the matching clauses, so a 150-page contract never goes into one prompt. Each finding must quote clause text, and code checks the quote and number against the document; unmatched findings are dropped and logged, and poorly scanned pages are flagged. Retrieval is scoped to one client's playbook and one matter, with no shared index. The associate reviews and the partner signs off; nothing goes to the client automatically. We keep the contract version, playbook version, findings and edits for each memo. On 50 associate-labelled contracts, I'd want 90% issue recall and 100% citation accuracy before launch.
answers.why: Verifies every citation in code, keeps clients apart, feeds only relevant clauses into context, keeps associates and partners in control and sets recall and citation bars.

answers.text: I'd ask how the memo is structured and who reviews it. The agent takes a contract, compares each clause with the client's playbook and writes findings that quote the exact clause text from the document, so associates can check them. Each client gets its own playbook store, and the agent's access is limited to that client's matter. The associate edits the draft memo and a partner signs off before anything reaches the client. I'd also show preferred and fallback positions side by side, so associates can decide quickly.
answers.why: Keeps clients apart and humans in charge, but quotes are never checked by code, there is no plan for long contracts or poor scans, no version history and no measure of review quality.

answers.text: I'd use a strong LLM with a large context window. We paste in the contract and the client's playbook and ask it to produce a review memo with clause citations. We'd add guardrails against hallucination and prompt it to be careful and precise. It could also suggest better wording for each clause, and over time we could fine-tune it on our past memos. It should save a lot of time compared with manual review.
answers.why: Stuffs the whole contract into one prompt, trusts model-written citations, mentions no client separation, no checks, no logging and no evaluation.

listen.text: Is every clause number and quote checked by code against the actual document?
What goes into context for a 150-page contract, and what stays out?
How is one client's contract and playbook kept away from another client's review?
Is quality measured as recall against associate labels, with citation accuracy at 100%?

answers.text: Can I check how many clients' playbooks we hold, and whether the memo covers every clause or only deviations? I'll assume deviations. Each client gets a separate index and credentials scoped to that client, so a review can't retrieve another client's text. I'd chunk by clause, then use hybrid search — keyword for defined terms, embeddings for meaning — to match each playbook rule to at most five clauses. That keeps context near 8,000 tokens even for 150 pages. Citations are inserted by code from the chunk metadata, never typed by the model. If a page's OCR confidence is low, its findings are marked 'verify manually'. The memo goes to the associate, then the partner for sign-off. I'd measure recall against associate flags on 40 past contracts, targeting 85%, and track the partner edit rate.
answers.why: Different angle: hybrid retrieval, per-client indexes and a tight context budget, with citations from metadata. It never says what is recorded per memo, so the audit trail is missing.

answers.text: I'd ask how long contracts run and what the confidentiality rules are. I'd split each contract into clauses by its headings and work clause by clause, sending the model only the clauses relevant to each playbook rule, so even 150 pages fits a small context. Each client has its own index, and the agent's credentials only reach that client's matter. Clause numbers and quotes in the memo are inserted from the parsed document, not written by the model. The memo lists each deviation with the preferred and fallback positions.
answers.why: Avoids all three traps, but no associate or partner sign-off, no handling of poor scans or unmatched findings, no version history and no way to measure review quality.

answers.text: First, the memo format and who signs off. I'd build one firm-wide vector index of every contract and playbook we've ever reviewed, because precedent is our edge: when reviewing a clause, the agent retrieves similar clauses and positions from all past matters, which makes suggestions far richer. Findings quote the clause text, and code verifies each quote against the document. The associate reviews and the partner signs off. I'd measure issue recall against associate-labelled contracts, targeting 90%, and track the partner edit rate.
answers.why: Persuasive about precedent, but one shared index across clients is the second trap: client A's contracts and playbook can surface in client B's memo, breaching confidentiality.

listen.text: Does retrieval handle defined terms and exact clause wording, for example with keyword search?
Does the candidate combine keyword and semantic search to match playbook rules to clauses?
Would the candidate offer tracked suggestions rather than silent redlines?
Are retrieved passages limited to the current client and matter?

answers.text: I'd start by asking what engineers actually want flagged, how big PRs get and what the CI runner can reach. With 1,500 PRs a week, noise kills adoption, so I'd post only high-confidence findings, each pinned to an exact line with a reproducing test where possible. The agent runs in a sandbox with read-only repo access and a token scoped to commenting and pushing to that one PR branch; the staging deploy credentials never enter it. Fix-ups land only if the author accepts them, and humans still approve merges. If the model times out, it posts 'review unavailable' rather than blocking the PR. Every review, file read and tool call is logged. For 2,000-line diffs, I review changed hunks plus their callers under a per-PR token cap. Launch bar: 60% comment acceptance on labelled past PRs.
answers.why: Covers everything: scoped token with no deploy secrets, author acceptance for fix-ups, line-level evidence, a timeout fallback, logging, a token cap for huge diffs and a measurable launch bar.

answers.text: I'd ask about typical PR sizes and which languages we need to support. The flow is simple: a webhook fires on each PR, the agent reads the diff, calls the model and posts comments that quote the exact file and line they refer to. It gets a token that can only comment and push to the PR's own branch. For big PRs, I'd split the diff by file, review each file separately and cap the whole review at about 50,000 tokens so cost stays predictable. Style issues it can fix directly with a small commit.
answers.why: Sensible flow with a scoped token and a token cap, but no evaluation of noise, no author acceptance for fix-ups, no logging and no plan for model failures.

answers.text: I'd plug a large language model into the CI pipeline. When a pull request opens, we send the diff to the model and ask it to find bugs, security problems and style issues, then post them as comments. It can also commit fixes. I'd add guardrails so it doesn't do anything bad, and write a good system prompt telling it to be helpful and concise. Over time we could fine-tune it on our codebase so the reviews get smarter, and engineers will save a lot of review time.
answers.why: Generic 'send the diff to a model' with vague guardrails. No questions, no scoped credentials, no evidence per comment, no evaluation and nothing about noise or cost.

listen.text: Keeps deploy credentials out of the reviewer's environment; its token covers comments and one PR branch.
Treats PR descriptions and code comments as untrusted data, never as instructions.
Measures usefulness with comment acceptance and false positives, because engineers ignore noisy bots.
Bounds cost on huge diffs: changed hunks plus neighbours and a token cap per PR.

answers.text: Before designing, I'd check what share of PRs come from outside contributors and whether the CI runner is shared with deploy jobs. If it is, the reviewer gets its own runner with no secrets, just a repo read token and a comment-only token. I'd build a fixed workflow rather than a free agent: a cheap classifier skips trivial PRs like lockfile bumps, which trims a good slice of the 1,500 weekly, the main model reviews file by file, and a small filter model drops low-confidence remarks. Fixes go out as suggested changes the author clicks to apply. Tool calls, inputs and outputs go to a review log. If the model errors, we retry once, then post nothing. We ship when engineers rate 70% of comments on 300 historical PRs useful.
answers.why: Different angle: threat-model questions, a secret-free runner, a classifier and filter to cut noise and cost, author-applied suggestions, logging, a failure rule and a numeric launch bar.

answers.text: I'd ask which languages and what review standards the team already has written down. The agent reads the diff alongside the team's style guide and posts comments that cite the file and line, so nobody has to guess what it means. To keep the noise down it posts at most five comments per PR, ranked by severity. For evaluation, I'd take 200 past PRs where reviewers found real bugs and measure how many the agent catches, aiming for at least half before we switch it on for everyone.
answers.why: Good on noise and a measurable bar, but silent on credentials and the deploy secrets, on who accepts fix-ups, on logging, on failure handling and on cost for large diffs.

answers.text: I'd start by confirming volume, about 1,500 PRs a week, and the size of the largest diffs. The agent runs as a step inside the existing CI job, which is elegant: it inherits the runner's environment, so it can build the branch, push fix-ups and even trigger the staging deploy to confirm a fix really works end to end. Comments cite exact lines and the failing test output. To keep cost flat, it reviews only changed hunks and caps each PR at 40,000 tokens. We'd measure comment acceptance on 200 labelled past PRs, aiming for 65%.
answers.why: Fluent and measured, but it falls into the trap of running with the runner's deploy credentials; one injected PR description could reach staging. Also no author acceptance, logging or failure handling.

listen.text: Names the threat model: outside contributors write text the agent will read.
Defines tool contracts: comment, suggest, push to one branch; nothing else is allowed.
Runs the reviewer in its own sandbox, separate from runners that hold deploy secrets.
Sets a noise budget: a few high-confidence comments beat many nits.

answers.text: I'd first ask which questions users ask most, how they check a number today and how row-level security is enforced. The pilot gave plausible wrong numbers, so the agent shouldn't invent joins: it picks from a semantic layer of approved metrics and join paths, and the data team signs off any new metric before it's usable. Queries run on a read-only connection as the user, so their row rules apply. Before execution I validate the SQL, add a row limit and check the cost estimate; a sanity check flags totals that jump after a join. Each answer stores the question, SQL, row count and user. For the 10-second target, I retrieve candidate tables from schema descriptions, cache frequent queries and stream the explanation. Release needs 90% execution accuracy on 400 real questions.
answers.why: Complete: approved metrics instead of invented joins, data-team sign-off, queries run as the user, pre-run validation and join checks, logging, a latency plan and execution accuracy with a bar.

answers.text: I'd ask how many users there are and how fast answers need to be. Then I'd embed the table descriptions, retrieve the top ten tables for each question and give their schemas to the model, which writes the SQL. We run it and the model describes the result and suggests a chart. The connection is read-only and uses each user's own credentials, so row-level security holds. To stay under ten seconds I'd cache results for repeated questions per company and use a smaller model just for picking tables.
answers.why: Right access model and a latency plan, but the model still writes joins from raw schemas, which caused the pilot's wrong numbers. No SQL checks, no evaluation and no logging.

answers.text: I'd use an LLM with the database schema in the prompt. The user asks a question in plain English, the model generates SQL, we run it against the warehouse and show a chart. To stop wrong numbers I'd tell the model to double-check its work and use the strongest model available. We'd add guardrails for security. It should be fast enough, since modern models are quick. Once it's live we can keep improving the prompt as people use it.
answers.why: Repeats the pilot that failed: raw schema in a prompt and 'double-check your work'. No access model, no approved metrics, no validation, no evaluation and no latency plan.

listen.text: Stops the model inventing joins: it chooses approved metrics and join paths from a semantic layer.
Runs queries as the user so the warehouse enforces row-level security; no shared account.
Scores execution accuracy on real questions with verified results, not how the SQL reads.
Meets ten seconds with table retrieval, query caching and a cached schema prefix.

answers.text: My first question is what counts as right: matching the finance dashboard, or just a sensible query? I'd also ask which 30 tables carry most questions. I'd build the gold set first: 500 real questions from the pilot logs, each with SQL a data engineer verified, scored by comparing result sets, not SQL text, with 92% to launch. The agent composes queries from curated metric definitions rather than raw joins. It runs through a read-only role that impersonates the user, so the warehouse enforces row-level security. If a query errors, it gets one repair attempt using the error message; after that it says it couldn't answer. Every question, query and result size is logged per user. For latency, the 30 core tables sit in a cached prompt prefix and common metric queries are memoised.
answers.why: Evaluation-first angle: a verified gold set scored on results with a bar, curated metrics, user-scoped read-only access, a bounded repair loop, per-user logging and prefix caching for speed.

answers.text: I'd ask what access model each client company uses. The core is a semantic layer: approved metrics and join paths, and the model maps each question onto those instead of writing joins itself. It queries through the user's own read-only login, so row-level security applies. Then it shows the numbers with a chart and a short note saying which metric it used. I'd log each question, the generated SQL and who asked, so the data team can look into odd results. Later I'd add more metrics as users ask for them.
answers.why: Safe core with approved metrics, user-scoped access and logging, but no evaluation set, no SQL validation or join sanity checks, and no plan for the 10-second target.

answers.text: I'd confirm the ten-second target and the questions users ask most. The design uses a semantic layer of approved metrics so the model never improvises joins. To keep things simple and fast, all queries run through one pooled service account with read access to the whole warehouse, and the agent adds a filter on the user's company to each query. Common queries are cached to stay under ten seconds. We'd score it on 500 real questions by comparing result sets, targeting 90%.
answers.why: Polished, but it falls into the shared-service-account trap: row-level security is bypassed and a model-written filter is all that separates 50 client companies. No failure handling or logging either.

listen.text: Validates SQL before running: read-only, row limit, cost estimate, checks for duplicating joins.
Finds the right tables among 400 with hybrid search over schema descriptions.
Treats a shared service account as a data-leak risk across 50 client companies.
Asks how users verify numbers today, since plausible wrong totals sank the pilot.

answers.text: I'd ask about volume, how often articles change, how plans differ and when a human must take over. With 50,000 questions a day, I'd use hybrid keyword and vector search over current articles only, re-indexed when an article is published, filtered by the customer's plan and version. Past tickets only help match questions, never supply answers. The agent reads this customer's plan and settings and nothing from other accounts. Refunds, billing changes and data deletion are decided by a human; the bot hands over a summary. If retrieval confidence is low, it says so and offers a handoff. Each answer logs article IDs and versions. I'd require retrieval recall@5 above 90%, measured separately from groundedness. A semantic cache and a small routing model keep first token under two seconds.
answers.why: Full coverage: fresh, plan-filtered hybrid retrieval, account-scoped access, humans deciding refunds and deletions, an honest low-confidence path, version logging, separate retrieval metrics and caching for latency.

answers.text: First I'd ask about volume and the latency target. I'd chunk and embed all 8,000 articles into a vector database, pull the top five chunks per question and have the model answer with a link to the article it used. I'd put a cache in front for the most common questions, since many of the 50,000 daily questions repeat. If nothing relevant comes back, it says it doesn't know and offers to open a ticket for the team.
answers.why: Reasonable RAG with a cache and a safe fallback, but it ignores plan differences and freshness, has no account scoping, no human decisions on billing, no logging and no evaluation.

answers.text: I'd put all the help articles and past tickets into a vector database and use RAG with an LLM. The model reads the top results and writes a friendly answer for the customer. If they're not happy, they can ask for a human. I'd add guardrails so it stays on topic, and pick a fast model so it responds quickly. We'd test it with the support team before launch and then roll it out to everyone.
answers.why: Generic RAG that indexes outdated tickets as truth and ignores plans. No clarifying questions, no freshness plan, no scoping, no metrics and no concrete latency technique.

listen.text: Keeps the index fresh: re-indexes on article change so yesterday's version is never quoted.
Filters retrieval by the customer's plan and version, since the right answer depends on who asks.
Evaluates retrieval recall separately from answer groundedness instead of one quality score.
Names what gets cached at 50,000 questions a day and the cost per resolved question.

answers.text: Two questions first: how fast must an article edit reach answers, and does the ticket system know the customer's plan? I'd make freshness an event: when an article is published, its old chunks are deleted and new ones embedded within minutes, each tagged with plan and version. Old tickets are mined only for common phrasings, not answers. Retrieval is filtered by the signed-in customer's plan via a read-only lookup for that account alone. I'd evaluate in two layers: recall@10 on 1,000 labelled questions must stay above 85%, and a calibrated judge scores groundedness separately. When the top score is weak, the bot says it's unsure and hands over. Answers log article versions. A semantic cache catches repeats and prompt caching protects the 2-second first token.
answers.why: Freshness-first angle: event-driven re-indexing, tickets kept out of answers, account-scoped plan lookup, two-layer evaluation with bars, an unsure-and-hand-over path, logging and caching for latency.

answers.text: I'd ask which plans exist and which issues must always go to a person. Retrieval uses only the current help articles, filtered to the customer's plan, so we never describe a feature they don't have, and each answer links its article. Refund requests and suspected security incidents go to a human who decides, with the conversation attached. If the search comes back empty or the model times out, the customer gets a clear message and a ticket is opened automatically.
answers.why: Handles plans, refunds and failures well, but gives no evaluation or metrics, no logging of sources, no account scoping and no plan for 50,000 a day inside two seconds.

answers.text: I'd confirm volume, around 50,000 a day, and the two-second first-token target. Our richest source is years of resolved tickets, so I'd index all of them alongside the 8,000 articles and weight ticket answers highly, because agents' real replies capture edge cases the articles miss. A semantic cache handles repeated questions and a small model routes intents, which comfortably meets the latency budget. I'd log every answer with the sources it drew on.
answers.why: Confident and fast, but it treats old tickets as truth, so outdated answers get quoted with authority. It also ignores plan differences, has no evaluation and no handoff rule.

listen.text: Rejects fine-tuning on tickets as the fix: it bakes in stale answers and cannot cite.
Meets the two-second first token with prompt-prefix caching and streaming.
Combines keyword and vector search so product names and error codes match exactly.
Hands off when retrieval confidence is low, rather than guessing.

answers.text: I'd ask what exactly triggers payment, how often the portal changes and what error rate the client tolerates. Before entry, extracted fields are matched against the purchase order and supplier master; mismatches go to a queue. The agent works in an isolated browser with a portal login that can enter invoices but not approve payments; a person approves each payment batch, and new suppliers or bank-detail changes always need a human. Each invoice is a resumable task: after a session expiry it searches the portal for the invoice number before re-entering, so no duplicates. Screenshots, actions and extracted data are stored per invoice. Stable screens use fixed selectors; the vision agent runs only when a layout check fails. Go-live needs 98% task success on 500 labelled invoices replayed on a portal copy.
answers.why: Complete: PO and supplier matching, an entry-only login with human payment approval, duplicate-safe resumption, per-invoice evidence, selector-first automation for cost and a replay test with a bar.

answers.text: I'd ask how many invoices come in, what happens after entry and how often the layout changes. An extraction step reads each PDF into fields, and a computer-use agent logs into the portal and types them in. It gets a dedicated portal account with entry rights only, no payment approval. We'd store a screenshot after each step so any invoice can be reviewed later. With 3,000 a day, screenshots add up, so I'd script the stable screens with fixed selectors and use the vision model only on screens whose layout changes.
answers.why: Sound account limits and cost thinking, but no PO or supplier checks, no duplicate check after a session expiry, no measured success rate and nothing on phishing or new suppliers.

answers.text: I'd use one of the new computer-use models. It reads each invoice email, opens the portal and fills in the invoice the way a person would. Since it looks at the screen, layout changes don't really matter. I'd add guardrails against phishing and monitor it closely for the first few weeks. This could save the client a lot of staff time and cut the backlog. The model reads PDFs well, so extraction should be accurate, and the whole thing could be running within a month.
answers.why: Trusts a general agent with a money-moving task: no account limits, no human approval, no PO matching, no duplicate handling, no evaluation and only vague guardrails.

listen.text: Separates entry from payment approval: the agent's portal role cannot approve.
Checks the portal for an existing entry before retrying after a session timeout.
Treats invoice emails, including hidden text, as data, never as instructions.
Measures task success on a portal copy with labelled invoices before trusting it.

answers.text: My first question is who can reject a scheduled payment in those three days, because that's our safety net. I'd design around it: the agent's portal role can create invoices but has no approve permission, and a clerk reviews a daily batch screen showing each invoice with its checks. Any sender-domain mismatch, new supplier or changed bank account is held for a human. Invoices are entered only when amount, PO number and supplier match the ERP records. Hidden text or instructions in emails are ignored; the extractor outputs fixed fields only. After a timeout, the task resumes by searching for the invoice number first. Every click is recorded with screenshots. We'd trial on a portal copy with 500 real invoices, requiring 99% field accuracy, then shadow-run for two weeks.
answers.why: Control-design angle: an entry-only role, clerk batch approval, holds on new suppliers and bank changes, ERP matching, duplicate-safe resumption, click-level evidence and a strict trial bar.

answers.text: I'd ask what error rate the client accepts and whether we can get a test copy of the portal. Each invoice's fields are checked against the purchase order and the supplier list before anything is typed. The agent uses a portal account limited to entering invoices. We'd measure it on 300 historical invoices replayed against the test copy, and require 97% entered with every field correct before going live. I'd start with one supplier group and expand from there.
answers.why: Good checks and a measured bar, but nothing on duplicates after session expiry, no human approval for new suppliers or bank changes, no per-invoice evidence and no cost plan for screenshots.

answers.text: I'd confirm volume, 3,000 a day, and how often the layout moves. Each invoice is matched against its purchase order before entry. Sessions are handled as resumable tasks: after a timeout the agent searches for the invoice number before retrying, so we never double-enter. Every step is screenshotted. And since the three-day hold only delays suppliers, the agent's account would also approve payment once the PO match passes, saving the client a day and removing a manual step.
answers.why: Well engineered, but it hands the agent payment approval, so the same actor enters and approves money. That removes the one human control; a convincing phishing invoice with a matching PO gets paid.

listen.text: Combines fixed selectors for stable screens with screen understanding when layouts change.
Keeps screenshot cost down by calling the vision model only when a layout check fails.
Sends new suppliers and bank-detail changes to a human every time.
Plans a weekly staff-checked sample after launch, not just a one-off test.

answers.text: I'd ask about document volume, how permissions are modelled, how versions are marked and which answers affect customers. Permissions stay in the document system, so retrieval filters by the user's live access at query time, before any text reaches the model. Only the current version of each policy is searchable, and answers cite it with its effective date. For customer-affecting topics like complaints or fees, staff must get the policy owner's sign-off before acting, and the answer names that owner. If sources conflict or confidence is low, it says it's unsure and lists them. Questions, retrieved documents and answers are logged for compliance. I'd re-embed only changed documents and cache common answers per role. Before launch, leak tests across six roles must surface zero restricted documents.
answers.why: Covers it all: live permission filtering before the model, current versions with dates, owner sign-off on customer-affecting answers, an unsure path, compliance logging, incremental indexing and a zero-leak bar.

answers.text: I'd ask how many documents there are and how often policies change. I'd index the policy library in a vector store, tag each chunk with version and effective date, and exclude superseded versions so answers cite the current policy. If nothing matches well, it says so rather than guessing. All questions and answers are logged for compliance review. It would sit on the intranet as a simple chat window that staff in all 12 countries can reach.
answers.why: Handles versions and uncertainty, but never says how permissions reach retrieval, so restricted content could leak. No leak testing, no sign-off for high-impact answers and no indexing cost plan.

answers.text: I'd load all the policy documents into a vector database and build a chatbot with RAG. Staff type a question, it finds the relevant text and the LLM answers. For restricted content we can add guardrails. It should be much better than asking colleagues. We'd pilot it with one team and gather feedback before rolling it out across the bank. The model is good at summarising, so answers will be clear, and we can add more document types later.
answers.why: One store with 'guardrails' for restricted content: no permission model, no version control, no citations, no logging and no testing. It would leak restricted and superseded policies.

listen.text: Filters by the user's live permissions at retrieval, before any text reaches the model.
Excludes superseded policies and cites the current version with its effective date.
Logs question, retrieved documents and answer so compliance can review them.
Uses metadata filters for role, country and effective date inside the vector query.

answers.text: First: where do permissions live, and how quickly must a revocation take effect? If access goes at 10 am, a question at 10:05 must not see that folder. So I wouldn't copy permissions into the index nightly; each chunk carries its document ID, and at query time we check the user's current groups against the document system, cached for at most a minute. If that service is unreachable, the assistant refuses rather than using older access data. Filtering happens at retrieval, never on the answer. Superseded policies drop out when a new effective date arrives, and answers quote the policy number and date. Each query records the user, document IDs and answer. Testing: 400 red-team questions run as twelve personas; one restricted passage blocks release. Only changed documents are re-embedded, from the change feed, never all 60,000.
answers.why: Revocation-first angle: live permission checks at retrieval, a refuse-on-outage rule, current versions only, per-query logging, persona-based leak tests as a hard gate and change-feed indexing.

answers.text: I'd ask how many countries are involved and whether some policies differ by country. Retrieval applies the user's current permissions from the document system as a filter, so restricted text never reaches the model. Each chunk is tagged with country and version, only current versions are indexed, and answers cite the policy and its effective date. I'd log each question, the documents used and the answer for the compliance team. The front end would sit on the intranet.
answers.why: Right permission and version design, but no leak testing or evaluation, no behaviour for low confidence or conflicting sources, no sign-off for customer-affecting answers and no indexing plan.

answers.text: I'd confirm the corpus, about 60,000 documents, and how versions are marked. For simplicity and recall, I'd index everything into one store and let the model draw on the full library; then a policy check inspects the cited documents and removes any answer that relies on a restricted source before it's shown. Superseded versions are excluded and answers cite the effective date. Common questions are cached, and only changed documents are re-embedded rather than all 60,000.
answers.why: Sounds efficient, but it filters after generation: restricted text has already reached the model and can leak into an answer through uncited wording. No logging, leak tests or sign-off either.

listen.text: Proves no leakage with red-team questions run as users in different roles.
Keeps index cost down at 60,000 documents with incremental embedding and compact vectors.
Combines keyword and vector search so policy numbers and circular IDs match exactly.
Shows sources and says 'not sure' when policies conflict, instead of picking one.

answers.text: I'd ask what the team knows well, where it must deploy, the deadlines and what made the prototype hard to debug. My recommendation: a plain Python SDK loop for the support agent, not a heavy framework, with shared pieces built once. A model gateway on their cloud account routes simple support intents to a small model, tracks cost per agent and fails over to a second provider on timeouts. A tool gateway holds per-agent credentials: the analysis agent gets read-only warehouse access, the sales agent CRM reads only. Each agent answers from its own systems: help centre, warehouse, CRM. Tracing records every model and tool call from day one. One evaluation harness, a test set per agent, and a release gate at 85% task success. Fine-tuning waits for evidence.
answers.why: Requirements before tools, a plain loop, shared gateways with routing, failover and scoped credentials, grounding per agent, tracing and one evaluation gate. Misses human approval steps for actions like sales outreach.

answers.text: I'd ask why the prototype is hard to debug and what the deadlines are. I'd drop the current framework and pick a graph-based one that makes state explicit, and use it for all three agents so the team learns one tool. I'd add tracing across all of them from the start so every step is visible. Each agent gets a test set of 200 real cases and must pass 80% before release. On fine-tuning, I'd hold off for now and start with prompting.
answers.why: One stack with tracing and a release bar, but no shared gateway, no per-agent permissions, no grounding in each agent's systems, no provider failover and no cost control.

answers.text: I'd go with the most popular agent framework, since it has the biggest community and integrations for everything. We'd build all three agents on it, starting with support. For the CTO, yes, fine-tuning our own model makes sense long term so we own our AI, and we could start collecting data now. Add guardrails and monitoring, and we should be fine for the timeline. The framework also ships ready-made agent templates, so the team can move quickly and deliver all three well before the deadline.
answers.why: Picks a framework by popularity before any requirements and endorses fine-tuning first. No shared platform pieces, permissions, evaluation or tracing; nothing measurable.

listen.text: Justifies a plain SDK loop or a light framework by debuggability, not popularity.
Builds shared pieces once: model gateway, tool gateway, tracing, evaluation harness.
Answers the fine-tuning question with data: prompt and retrieve first, fine-tune a measured gap.
Defines governance before the third agent: an owner, a release checklist, approval steps.

answers.text: Before choosing tools, I'd pin down success: at three months, the support agent resolving 40% of tickets with groundedness above 90% on a 300-case set; at nine months, all three live on one platform. I'd also ask what failed in the prototype. Shared platform first: one model gateway on their cloud account for provider switching, retries and timeouts; one tool gateway issuing scoped credentials per agent; one trace store for every call. The sales-research agent may draft outreach, but a rep approves before anything is sent. Support answers from the help centre, analysis from the warehouse. Each agent has an owner and a release checklist. The gateway routes simple support intents to a small model and caches the system-prompt prefix.
answers.why: Outcome-first angle: measurable targets at 3 and 9 months, a shared platform with failover, scoped credentials and tracing, rep approval on outreach, grounding per agent and routing plus prefix caching.

answers.text: I'd start by asking about deadlines, deployment rules and the team's languages. Since they're mostly Python, I'd standardise on one Python stack for all three agents. Each agent reads from its own source: the help centre for support, the warehouse for analysis and the CRM for sales research. Each gets its own service credentials with only the access it needs. On fine-tuning, I'd tell the CTO to start with prompting and retrieval and revisit it later.
answers.why: Sensible single stack with grounding and scoped credentials, but no evaluation harness, no tracing, no provider failover, no approval steps and no cost plan.

answers.text: I'd clarify the deadlines and deployment limits first. Given we must run on our own cloud, the durable move is to fine-tune an open-weights model in month one and host it ourselves; that removes provider lock-in and gives us a model that knows our product. All three agents then share it through one gateway with per-agent credentials, and shared tracing logs every call. The support agent follows once the model is trained.
answers.why: Polished platform talk, but it fine-tunes first, before any evaluation shows a gap, burning the three-month support deadline on training. No evaluation set, fallback or approval steps.

listen.text: Versions prompts, tools and models so each release can be compared and rolled back.
Explains when an explicit graph framework earns its place over a plain loop.
Avoids lock-in with one model gateway, so adding a second provider is configuration.
Treats owned evaluation data as the durable asset, not a fine-tuned model.
